terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Write a form body
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/forms.js`, make `formBody(fields)` take an object of names and values, like `{ song: 'Weather for Ducks', from: 'Bram, who is nine' }`, and give back the text of the body a form sends for them, in the same order. Every value must arrive as typed, also when it has `&`, `=`, `+` or `%` in it. For an empty object it gives back empty text.

Check calls `formBody` with fields of its own and reads the text it gives back the way a server reads a form body.
nextSteps: Find in the lesson what a form body looks like, and which object writes it.
Make that object from the fields.
Give back its text, not the object.
Run `node run.js` and look at how the `&` in the name was written.
hints: A form body is written exactly like the question mark part of an address, with the same codes for characters that have a job.
`URLSearchParams` can start from an object of names and values, and encodes each value for you. Its `toString()` writes the text.

tasks.title: Send the request form
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `sendRequestForm(base, fields)` send `fields` to the server at `base` the way the website's request form does: a `POST` to `/forms/request` whose body is a form body, with the content type of a form body. It gives back the text of the answer's body, whatever the status.

Check starts a server of its own and looks at the method, the `content-type` and the body its server received, and at the text `sendRequestForm` gave back.
nextSteps: Hand `fetch` the method and a form body in its options.
Make sure the request says it carries a form body: print it, or read the request `run.js` shows.
Read the body of the answer as text and give it back.
Run `node run.js`: one slip is for a song that is already on the list.
hints: The server takes this form only as a form body, labelled with the long content type the lesson names. Anything else gets 415.
Handed a `URLSearchParams` as its body, `fetch` writes the text and adds the right `content-type` by itself. Handed text, it labels it as plain text.
`fetch(new URL('/forms/request', base), { method: 'POST', body: new URLSearchParams(fields) })`, then `return await response.text()`.

docs.title: Using the Fetch API: setting a body

tasks.title: Send a jingle entry with its file
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `enterJingle(base, entrant, fileName, script)` send a jingle entry to the server at `base` the way the website's jingle form does: a `POST` to `/forms/jingle` whose body is `multipart/form-data` with two parts:

- `entrant`, a plain value: the entrant's name
- `script`, a file called `fileName` whose contents are `script`

It gives back the text of the answer's body.

Check starts a server of its own, finds the parts in the body its server received, and looks at each part's name, file name and contents.
nextSteps: Make the object the lesson uses to hold the parts of a form.
Add the entrant's name, then the script as a file with its file name.
Hand that object to `fetch` as the body, and leave the `content-type` alone.
Run `node run.js` and read the parts in the body it prints.
hints: A file needs a body made of parts. `fetch` writes one for you from a `FormData`, boundary and all.
`append` takes a name and a value. For a file, the value is a `Blob` made from the contents, and the file name goes third. Setting a `content-type` yourself loses the boundary.
`form.append('entrant', entrant)` and `form.append('script', new Blob([script], { type: 'text/plain' }), fileName)`, then `fetch(new URL('/forms/jingle', base), { method: 'POST', body: form })`.
